HEICO · Jet Avion · Summer 2026

Spring Fatigue Tester

The Goal

Design a spring fatigue-testing machine that tests two springs at once until they fail, to cut outsourced testing costs and time, and to generate reliable data.

Who, What, Where.

As a New Product Development intern at HEICO's Jet Avion in summer 2026, I joined a team developing a stronger replacement for a brake-control spring used in the rudder-pedal assemblies of the Boeing 787-8/-9/-10 aircraft. They needed fatigue testing on these springs and outsourced testing was costly, took a significant amount of time, and provided unreliable test data. My task was to design a testing machine that could be used in-house. 

1 · Capability

Able to test two or more springs at once, with an adjustable 1–4" stroke length and a 500 rpm target speed.

2 · Durability

Cycles each spring until it breaks, giving the team real fatigue-life data in-house.

3 · Cost

Whole machine cost about $10,000, which was the price of a single outsourced test.

How It Works

1. Drive

A three-phase 2 hp motor on a VFD turns a pulley through a V-belt with a 3:1 reduction.

2. Convert

The pulley spins a crank. The crank arm turns rotation into linear motion, pushing a slider with springs attached, on linear guide rails.

3. Load

Two springs run between the slider and a fixed fixture, stretching every revolution until they fail.

An adjustable crank slot sets the stroke anywhere from 1" to 4", so the same machine can run the standard test, or accelerated tests, for springs about 4.2" to 11.7" long.

Design Breakdown

The machine splits into five subassemblies. Each one mixes custom parts I designed in SolidWorks with catalogue parts.

Load Analysis

I sized the motor for the worst case: the accelerated test, with a 2" stroke at 500 rpm and a spring rate of 6,410 N/m.

Crank speed
ω = 2π · 50060 ≈ 52.4 rad/s
Torque and power
T = F r sin θ,  P = T ω
~640 Npeak force, springs plus inertia
8.3 N·mpeak crank torque
434 Wpeak power

About half the peak force comes from the springs at full stretch and half from accelerating the moving parts.

Design Decisions

  • Belt drive with a 3:1 reduction: more torque at the crank with a lower power motor that could still operate on a 120V outlet, and the belt absorbs shock when a spring breaks.
  • Two springs on one slider: twice the data per run, with balanced load on the guide shafts.
  • Adjustable crank radius: one machine can run several different types of springs with different test requirements.
  • 17-4 stainless and 6061 aluminum: stainless where parts see cyclic load and aluminum on the moving parts for less weight and less inertial force.

Requirements

RequirementTargetStatus
Speed500 rpmAwaiting test
CostUnder $15,000Met, ~$10k
Capacity2 or more springs at onceMet
PowerStandard 120 V outletMet
Size and weightFits within HEICO facility; can be carried by 2 peopleMet, 48 × 25 × 12 in

Current Status

The design was released and parts were made by the end of my internship. The team at Jet Avion is now assembling the machine.

Next: a cycle counter, a continuity circuit that detects a broken spring, then speed verification and durability testing.

Duke Pratt School of Engineering · 2025–26

AccessiBath

A portable bath that gives bedridden patients a real water-and-soap wash.

The Goal

Bedridden patients often only get sponge baths, which are undignified, often unhygienic and labor-intensive for caretakers. The goal: an accessible, comfortable way for patients to take a real bath.

Who, What, Where.

For our first-year design project, our team of four developed a bed bath concept inspired by our client, Lee Clayton, and his connection to The Forest at Duke, a retirement community in Durham, North Carolina. He wanted residents to experience a warm, comfortable bath that felt more like a traditional one. I designed the water system, including a custom pipe network, jets, and drainage.

1 · Clean

Pressurized jets with soap drawn in through a venturi valve to reach the whole body.

2 · Comfortable

An inclined mesh seat with a built-in hole for waste and a cushioned hair-wash basin to support the patient's body and head.

3 · Portable

A rolling frame with hose connection ports can connect to any water source while draining to an external tank.

The Water System

The system connects directly to an existing water source, draws soap in through a venturi attachment, sprays through adjustable jets in the tub walls, and carries waste water through a drain line to an external tank that is easy to empty.

  • Jets: gentle pressure with adjustable heads for different bath settings.
  • Retractable tarp: waterproof and adjustable with Velcro, so that water stays in the tub and the patient is exposed as little as possible.
  • Drainage: floor drain to an external tank, keeping waste away from the patient.

Testing

Each requirement became a pass/fail test with a numeric target, set before we built anything.

CriterionTestPass ifResult
Cleans all areasDoll coated in mud, sand and vinegar: 12 runsAverage ≥ 7Pass
ComfortSurvey on texture and appearance: 13 peopleAverage > 3Pass
Ease of useClassmates act as caretakers: 10 runsAverage > 3Pass
AdaptabilityLoads of different size and weight on the meshSag < 10 cmPass
Durability: tarpPull and close at three force levels: 20 runsNo breakagePass
Durability: frameIncreasing weight in the tub: 10 runsShift < 1 cmPass
Durability: mesh20 lb on the mesh for 2 hours: 3 runsSag < 2 cmPass

Duke AERO · Ground Systems · 2025 – present

RF Tracking Ground Station

An automatic two-axis antenna mount that follows our competition rocket in flight, replacing a station that was aimed by hand.

The Goal

Our Duke AERO rocket targets a 30,000 ft apogee in the IREC competition, the world's largest collegiate rocket engineering competition. At that range, it is impractical and difficult to manually operate and adjust an antenna based on the rocket's live location. So, the goal is to develop a ground station that tracks the rocket, receiving precise data throughout the whole flight, and moving the base and antenna accordingly.

System Operation

1 · Receive

Takes in the rocket's GPS telemetry over the radio link.

2 · Compute

Calculates the rocket's angle from the station in real time.

3 · Track

Drives two motors to keep the antennas pointed at the rocket as it climbs.

Current Design

  1. Base. A survey tripod supports a large plate that holds the electronics enclosure.
  2. Azimuth (θ). One motor rotates a smaller plate in the horizontal (x–y) plane, about the vertical axis. A thrust bearing between the plates carries the load.
  3. Elevation (φ). On the smaller plate, a motor and belt drive tilt a rod that carries the antennas up and down.

Onboard electronics calculate the rocket's angle from its telemetry, and encoders on each motor close the loop so the motors rotate to exactly the commanded position.

Analysis: Torque Required

Based on telemetry data from the 2025 IREC flight.

(1) Elevation rate
ωel = dφdt ≈ 28.28 °/s
(2) Azimuthal rate
ωaz = dθdt ≈ 21.96 °/s

Each antenna is modeled as a rod pivoting about its end, using its estimated mass and length.

AntennaMassMoment of inertia
Yagi, 433 MHz~0.8 kg0.327 kg·m²
Yagi, 915 MHz~0.8 kg0.131 kg·m²
Helical, 3.4 GHz~0.5 kg~0.015 kg·m² (preliminary)
Total~2.1 kg0.473 kg·m²
(3) Torque, with safety factor s = 2
τ = I · α · π180 · s
(4) Rod about its end
I = 13 m L2
(5) Angular acceleration
α = ΔωΔt
22.18 °/s²azimuthal acceleration
~0.37 N·mtorque required, azimuth
~0.29 N·mtorque required, elevation

The elevation acceleration is 17.28 °/s². The safety factor of 2 covers friction in the gearbox and bearings and other loads the equation leaves out. These are approximate numbers: the exact weights of the antennas and electronics on the station are not final yet.

Motor & Controller Selection

  • Elevation (φ): BLDC motor. Fast enough to keep up with the rocket during the initial boost.
  • Azimuth (θ): geared BLDC motor. The gear train turns the motor's high-speed, low-torque output into low-speed, high-torque, enough to rotate the plate with the antennas and electronics.
  • Two ODrive S1 motor controllers. Each drives one BLDC and reads its encoder, with torque, velocity, trajectory, and position control.

Next Steps

  • CAD: model the full design in Onshape.
  • Purchases: a survey tripod, a geared BLDC motor and two ODrive S1 motor controllers.
  • Prototype: build and test the small-scale proof of concept.
